- When sentiment is consistently negative (last 3–5 days), model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid excessive sell-off bias.  
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior peak), model often overshoots and fails to correct; reduce forecast peak by 5–10% and add a slight downward slope to avoid overreaction.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mildly positive, model underestimates upward momentum; increase forecast by 2–5% for next 3–5 periods to capture mean reversion toward higher levels.  
- Model frequently underestimates true price in early horizon (e.g., 1–3 days ahead) when sentiment is volatile; apply a 1–3% upward bias for short-term forecasts.  
- When sentiment shows strong upward momentum (e.g., >0.15 for 3+ days), model often fails to fully capture the rally; add 3–7% upward adjustment to forecast for 3–7 days ahead.  
- Model tends to underestimate true price in late horizon (e.g., 20+ days ahead) when sentiment is negative; apply a 2–5% upward bias to avoid premature mean reversion.  
- If sentiment is negative and price is trending upward, model often ignores the trend; add a slight upward bias to counteract sentiment-driven sell-off bias.  
- When sentiment is mixed or volatile, model tends to over-smooth price; use a 1–3% upward adjustment to capture short-term volatility.
